issues.description: font-weight HAS_NUMERIC regex has no case-insensitive flag but matches numeric strings — fine, but HAS_NAMED is case-insensitive while the value parser path later does its own case-folding. Mismatch worth a sanity check.
issues.detail: HAS_NAMED uses /i, HAS_NUMERIC does not. Numbers are case-agnostic so that's actually correct, but the asymmetry between the two regexes is the kind of thing the next maintainer will stare at for ten minutes. A one-line comment explaining 'numeric values are digits, no case flag needed' would save that time. Not a blocker.

issues.description: keyframe-selector-notation HAS_PERCENTAGE regex is missing the /i flag while HAS_KEYWORD has it — and the fallback selectorRegex = /./ is ugly.
issues.detail: PERCENTAGE_SELECTORS contains things like '0%' and '100%' — digits, no case issue, fine. But the `/./` fallback for the 'percentage-unless-within-keyword-only-block' branch is a code smell. It's saying 'match every rule' via a regex hack instead of either passing undefined or branching the walkRules call. walkRules with /./ still runs the regex test on every selector — pointless work. Either pass no filter for that branch, or restructure so the filter-less walk is its own call. Small refactor, real cleanup.

issues.description: selector-pseudo-element-colon-notation walkRules(/:/) will match attribute selectors like [href*=':'] and namespace selectors (svg|a), causing wasted parse work.
issues.detail: The previous code did `ruleNode.selector.includes(':')` which has the same false-positive surface — so this change is behavior-equivalent on that front. But moving the filter into walkRules' regex means it now runs against every rule's selector string the same way the old includes() did. Net: no regression, no real win on those false positives. The perf gain here is only from short-circuiting rules that have no colon at all. Fine as-is, but the commit message oversells it. Not a blocker.

issues.description: import-notation uses /url\(/i twice — extract or at least acknowledge the duplication.
issues.detail: Two adjacent lines test the same regex with opposite polarity. A const URL_FUNC = /url\(/i above would read better and compile once instead of twice (yes, V8 caches literals, but the intent matters). Minor taste issue.

issues.description: media-feature-range-notation: the 'context' regex /(?:min|max)-/i will match inside identifiers like --max-foo or custom prop names.
issues.detail: It's used as a fast-path filter — false positives just mean we don't skip — so correctness is preserved. But /(?:min|max)-/i is loose. Anchoring to a word boundary (`\b(?:min|max)-`) would skip more cases cheaply. Optional polish, not a blocker.

issues.description: No benchmark numbers in the PR description for a perf patch.
issues.detail: This is a performance PR titled 'Fix *-notation performance.' Where are the numbers? Before/after on a representative stylesheet would make this trivially acceptable. As-is, the reviewer has to take it on faith that pre-filtering with a regex beats the parser path. It almost certainly does, but a perf patch without measurements is talk, not code.

issues.description: Six rule changes in one patch — borderline THREE-PATCHES territory.
issues.detail: This touches six rules with the same shape of change. Defensible as one patch because the pattern is uniform and the changeset entry covers them collectively. But if any one of these regressions has to be reverted, the whole thing reverts together. A maintainer could reasonably ask for one commit per rule. Accepting it as one patch is fine; flagging the pattern for future PRs.

review.summary: NEEDS-WORK leaning ACCEPT. The shape of the patch is right: pre-filter with a cheap regex before calling the value/selector parser. That's exactly the kind of fast-path that makes a linter usable on real codebases. The taste is mostly good — except for the `/./` regex fallback in keyframe-selector-notation, which is the wrong shape (an always-true regex is a code smell; pass no filter or branch the walk call instead). Real complaint: this is a perf PR with zero numbers. Show me a before/after on a representative stylesheet and this lands clean. The selector-pseudo-element change is correctness-equivalent to the old includes(':') check, so it's a small win at best — don't oversell it. Six rules in one patch is borderline, but the uniformity justifies it. Fix the `/./` fallback, add benchmarks, ship it.
